content: 1. Primary HPV mRNA Screening (Screen-and-Treat Approach): For the general population of women, HPV mRNA testing is conducted using samples collected by a clinician. If the test result is negative, rescreening is recommended in five years. If the test result is positive, eligibility for ablative treatment is determined after applying 3–5% acetic acid, with or without magnification. If eligible for ablation, ablative treatment (e.g., cryotherapy or thermal ablation) is performed. If not eligible for ablation, LLETZ (large-loop excision of the transformation zone) or CKC (cold knife conization) is performed. If cancer is suspected, further evaluation, biopsy, and management are required. Post-treatment follow-up is conducted after one year, and rescreening is recommended every five years if no abnormalities are detected. 2. Primary HPV mRNA Screening with VIA Triage (Screen, Triage, and Treat Approach): In this approach, HPV mRNA testing is performed first. If the result is negative, rescreening is recommended in five years. If the result is positive, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) is used as a triage test. If VIA is negative, the HPV mRNA test is repeated after two years. If VIA is positive, eligibility for ablative treatment is assessed. Eligible cases undergo ablative treatment. Non-eligible cases are treated with LLETZ or CKC. If cancer is suspected, further evaluation, biopsy, and management are required. Post-treatment follow-up is conducted after one year. 3. Primary HPV mRNA Screening with Colposcopy Triage (Screen, Triage, and Treat Approach): HPV mRNA testing is performed, and if the result is negative, rescreening is recommended in five years. If the result is positive, colposcopy is used as a triage test. Further management is based on the colposcopy or histopathology diagnosis. Post-treatment follow-up is conducted after one year. 4. Primary HPV mRNA Screening with Cytology Triage Followed by Colposcopy (Screen, Triage, and Treat Approach): HPV mRNA testing is performed, and if the result is negative, rescreening is recommended in five years. If the result is positive, cytology is used as a triage test. If cytology is negative, the HPV mRNA test is repeated after two years. If cytology shows ASCUS (atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance) or worse, colposcopy is performed to determine further management. Post-treatment follow-up is conducted after one year. 5. Follow-Up Tests at 12 Months Post-Treatment: For women treated with ablation or LLETZ without histopathology results, or those treated based on histopathology findings of CIN 2/3 or AIS, follow-up testing is conducted within 12 months. If the follow-up test is negative, the patient returns to routine screening intervals based on the primary screening test. If the follow-up test is positive or cancer is suspected, further evaluation, biopsy, and management are required. Retreatment with LLETZ is recommended if necessary. In settings where LLETZ is unavailable, cryotherapy or thermal ablation may be used if the patient is eligible. 6. Recommendations for HPV DNA Testing and Other Cervical Screening Methods: The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test instead of VIA (visual inspection with acetic acid) or cytology in screening and treatment approaches for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. This recommendation is based on strong evidence with moderate certainty. Conditional recommendations are also provided, supported by moderate-certainty evidence, for specific contexts and populations. 7. Good Practice Statements: Screening and treatment recommendations are tailored to the general population of women and women living with HIV, emphasizing the importance of evidence-based approaches to improve outcomes and reduce the burden of cervical cancer.
